title: Types of Sentences
description: Learn sentence types by structure for Grade 7: simple, compound, complex and compound-complex sentences, with clauses and sentence-combining — bilingual notes, practice and tests.

topics.title: Simple & Compound Sentences
topics.concept:
A simple sentence has exactly one independent clause — one subject-verb idea that stands alone.

  • The baby slept. / Ravi and Sita went to the market. (still one clause, even with two subjects)

A compound sentence joins two or more independent clauses, each able to stand alone, using a coordinating conjunction (FANBOYS: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so) or a semicolon.

  • She studied hard, and she passed.
  • It was late; we went home.

Put a comma before the coordinating conjunction in a compound sentence.

examples.problem: Simple or compound? I like tea, but I prefer coffee.
Combine into a compound sentence: He was tired. He kept working.
examples.solution: He was tired, yet he kept working.

recap: Compound sentence = two+ independent clauses (FANBOYS or ;)
Use a comma before the coordinating conjunction

topics.title: Complex & Compound-Complex Sentences
topics.concept:
A complex sentence has one independent clause and one or more dependent (subordinate) clauses. A dependent clause begins with a subordinating conjunction (because, although, when, if, since, while, after, before) or a relative pronoun (who, which, that).

  • Although she was nervous, she spoke well. (dependent + independent)
  • The book that I read was excellent.

A compound-complex sentence has two or more independent clauses AND at least one dependent clause.

  • When the bell rang, the students left and the teacher locked the door.

Tip: put a comma after a dependent clause when it comes first.

examples.problem: Complex or compound-complex? Because it rained, we stayed in and played games.
examples.solution: Compound-complex — one dependent ('Because it rained') + two independent ('we stayed in', 'played games').

examples.problem: Combine into a complex sentence: He failed. He did not work hard.
examples.solution: He failed because he did not work hard.

recap: Comma after a leading dependent clause

questions.q: 'The cat slept.' is:
questions.explanation: One independent clause → simple.

questions.q: 'I tried, but I failed.' is:
questions.explanation: Two independent clauses + 'but' → compound.

questions.q: 'When it rained, we left.' is:
questions.explanation: Dependent + independent → complex.

questions.q: Which is a dependent clause?
questions.explanation: 'because he was late' cannot stand alone.

questions.q: Which conjunction makes a complex sentence?
questions.explanation: 'although' is subordinating.

questions.q: 'She sang and he danced.' is:
questions.explanation: Two independent clauses → compound.

questions.q: Identify the error type: 'It was hot we swam.'
questions.explanation: Two clauses with no joiner → run-on.

questions.q: 'Because she was kind' is a:
questions.explanation: A lone dependent clause is a fragment.

questions.q: Which is compound-complex?
options: When he ran, he won and smiled.
questions.explanation: 1 dependent + 2 independent clauses.

questions.q: Combine (compound): 'He was tired. He kept going.'
options: Although he was tired, he kept going.
He was tired, yet he kept going.
Because he was tired, he kept going.
He was tired he kept going.
questions.explanation: 'yet' (FANBOYS) makes it compound.

questions.q: Which sentence uses a semicolon correctly?
options: It was late; we went home.
It was late; and we went home.
It was late; so we left.
questions.explanation: A semicolon joins two related independent clauses without a conjunction.

questions.q: 'The boy who won is my friend.' is:
questions.explanation: 'who won' is a dependent (relative) clause → complex.

questions.q: Identify the structure: 'After the storm passed, the sun came out and the birds sang.'
questions.explanation: 1 dependent ('After the storm passed') + 2 independent clauses.

questions.q: Which sentence is correctly punctuated?
questions.explanation: Put a comma after a leading dependent clause.

questions.q: Combine into a complex sentence: 'He was honest. Everyone trusted him.'
options: He was honest, and everyone trusted him.
Because he was honest, everyone trusted him.
He was honest; everyone trusted him.
He was honest everyone trusted him.
questions.explanation: A subordinating conjunction makes it complex.

questions.q: Spot the comma splice.
options: I was hungry, so I ate.
Because I was hungry, I ate.
questions.explanation: Two independent clauses joined by only a comma = comma splice.

questions.q: Which clause is independent?
questions.explanation: 'the team won' stands alone as a complete thought.

questions.q: Reduce to a simple sentence: 'When she heard the news, she smiled.'
options: On hearing the news, she smiled.
She heard the news and she smiled.
Because she heard the news, she smiled.
questions.explanation: A participial/phrase reduction makes it a simple sentence.

questions.q: Rearrange into a compound-complex sentence: 'rang / when / the bell / we / left / and / went home'
options: When the bell rang, we left and went home.
We left when the bell rang and went home.
We went home and left when the bell rang.
The bell rang we left and went home.
questions.explanation: Dependent clause first, then two independent clauses.

questions.q: Which sentence has TWO dependent clauses?
options: Because he was tired and because it was late, he slept.
He was tired, so he slept.
He slept because he was tired.
questions.explanation: Two dependent 'because' clauses precede the independent clause.

outcomes: Tell apart simple, compound, complex and compound-complex sentences
Join independent clauses with coordinating conjunctions
Use subordinating conjunctions to build complex sentences
Combine short sentences into longer, varied ones

intro.en: We can sort sentences by their structure — by how many clauses they contain. A clause is a group of words with a subject and a verb. Learning the four structures (simple, compound, complex, compound-complex) lets you write with variety instead of a string of short, choppy sentences.
intro.hi: हम वाक्यों को उनकी संरचना के अनुसार बाँट सकते हैं — कि उनमें कितने उपवाक्य (clauses) हैं। उपवाक्य (clause) वह शब्द-समूह है जिसमें कर्ता और क्रिया हो। चार संरचनाएँ (simple, compound, complex, compound-complex) सीखकर आप छोटे-छोटे टूटे वाक्यों के बजाय विविधता से लिख पाते हैं।

real_life.situation:
Compare two ways of saying the same thing:

Choppy: It was raining. We stayed inside. We watched a film.

Better: Because it was raining, we stayed inside and watched a film.
real_life.why: The second version combines three short ideas into one smooth sentence using a subordinating conjunction ('because') and a coordinating one ('and'). Knowing sentence structures lets you write like this.

rule_box.html:
TypeClausesExample
Simple1 independentThe dog barked.
Compound2+ independentShe sang and he danced.
Complex1 independent + 1+ dependentWhen it rained, we left.
Compound-Complex2+ independent + 1+ dependentWhen it rained, we left and went home.
rule_box.formula: Independent clause = complete thought · Dependent clause = needs more
rule_box.example: Although he was tired (dependent), he finished the race (independent).

quick_test.explanation: A complex sentence has one independent clause plus at least one dependent clause.

common_mistakes.wrong: It was raining we stayed inside.
common_mistakes.right: It was raining, so we stayed inside.
common_mistakes.note: Two independent clauses need a conjunction or semicolon (avoid run-ons).

common_mistakes.right: Because he was late, he missed the bus.
common_mistakes.note: A dependent clause alone is a fragment; add a main clause.
A comma alone can't join two clauses (comma splice) — add 'and'.

common_mistakes.wrong: Although she was tired but she finished.
common_mistakes.right: Although she was tired, she finished.

fill_l1.instructions: Name the structure: simple, compound, or complex.

items.q: I called him, but he didn't answer.
When the rain stopped, we went out.
She smiled because she was happy.
He was ill. He went to school. (complex – although)
items.answer: Although he was ill, he went to school.

items.q: It was sunny. We went to the beach. (compound – so)
items.answer: It was sunny, so we went to the beach.

items.q: She studies daily. She scores well. (complex – because)
items.answer: Because she studies daily, she scores well.

items.q: The bell rang. We left. We took the bus. (compound-complex)
items.answer: When the bell rang, we left and took the bus.

items.q: He tried hard. He failed. (compound – but)
items.answer: He tried hard, but he failed.

error_detection.sentence: It was cold we stayed home.
error_detection.correct: It was cold, so we stayed home.
Because she was busy, she could not come.

error_detection.sentence: He ran fast, he won the race.
error_detection.correct: He ran fast, and he won the race.

error_detection.sentence: Although it rained but we played.

sentence_correction.wrong: I was tired I went to bed.
sentence_correction.correct: I was tired, so I went to bed.
When the show ended, everyone clapped.

rearrangement.jumbled: rained / because / it / we / stayed / inside
rearrangement.answer: Because it rained, we stayed inside.

rearrangement.jumbled: tired / although / he / was / he / continued
rearrangement.answer: Although he was tired, he continued.

answers: She sang and he danced. → compound
When it rained, we left. → complex
When it rained, we left and went home. → compound-complex

reading.passage: The match was about to begin. Because the captain was injured, the coach chose a new player, and the crowd cheered loudly. The new boy was nervous, but he played brilliantly. When the final whistle blew, our team had won, and everyone celebrated.

questions.q: Find a simple sentence in the passage.
questions.answer: "The match was about to begin." — one independent clause.

questions.q: Find a compound-complex sentence.
questions.answer: "Because the captain was injured, the coach chose a new player, and the crowd cheered loudly." — one dependent + two independent clauses.

questions.q: Identify the dependent clause in the last sentence.
questions.answer: "When the final whistle blew" — it begins with the subordinating conjunction 'when'.

speaking: I wanted to go, but it was too late. (compound)
Because she practised daily, she improved. (complex)
When the rain stopped, we went out and played. (compound-complex)
He is the boy who won the prize. (complex)

writing.prompt: Write four sentences about a holiday — one simple, one compound, one complex and one compound-complex.
writing.example: We reached the hills. It was cold, so we lit a fire. Because the view was lovely, we stayed. When night fell, we sang and slept under the stars.

micro_quiz.q: 'I read a book and she watched TV.' is:
micro_quiz.explanation: Two independent clauses joined by 'and' → compound.

options: He won because he ran fast.
micro_quiz.explanation: It has a dependent clause 'because he ran fast'.

micro_quiz.q: A group like 'although it was late' alone is a:
micro_quiz.explanation: A dependent clause alone is a fragment.

challenge.q: Identify the structure: 'Although he was rich, he lived simply, and he helped the poor.'
challenge.explanation: One dependent ('Although he was rich') + two independent clauses.

challenge.q: Which sentence is a comma splice (error)?
options: I came, I saw, I conquered.
challenge.explanation: Independent clauses joined by only commas form a comma splice.

challenge.q: Combine into a single complex sentence: 'The film was long. We enjoyed it.'
options: The film was long, and we enjoyed it.
Although the film was long, we enjoyed it.
The film was long; we enjoyed it.
The film was long we enjoyed it.
challenge.explanation: A subordinating conjunction ('Although') makes it complex.
